questions.stem: What is meant by ecological sustainability?
options: Using resources so that ecosystems stay healthy for the future
Using resources as quickly as possible while they are still available
Preventing every form of human use of natural ecosystems forever
Replacing native ecosystems with more productive farmland and forestry
questions.explanation: Ecological sustainability means meeting present needs while maintaining ecological processes, biodiversity and resources so that future generations can also meet theirs. It allows use, but not use that degrades the ecosystem.

questions.stem: Which practice best fits the principle of ecological sustainability in a fishery?
options: Increasing the catch each year as fishing boats become more efficient
Targeting the largest breeding adults, which provide the most meat
Allowing unlimited catches while the fish population still seems large
Setting catch limits below the population's replacement rate
questions.explanation: A sustainable catch removes fewer fish than are added by reproduction and growth, so the population persists. Removing the largest breeders reduces reproduction and can cause collapse.

questions.stem: Why is maintaining biodiversity central to ecological sustainability?
options: Diverse ecosystems are more resilient and keep providing services
Diverse ecosystems contain fewer species, so there is less competition for resources
Biodiversity stops all natural changes from happening in an ecosystem over time
Biodiversity matters only for tourism and has little part in ecosystem functioning
questions.explanation: Many species performing overlapping roles help an ecosystem recover from disturbance and keep supplying services such as pollination, clean water and soil formation. Diverse ecosystems still change over time.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of biosecurity at Australia's borders?
options: To stop exotic pests and diseases from entering and establishing
To stop native plants and animals from being taken overseas
To speed up the import of new crop varieties from overseas
To eradicate all pests already established across Australia
questions.explanation: Australia is free of many serious pests and diseases found elsewhere, so border biosecurity aims to keep them out, protecting agriculture, native species and human health. Managing pests already here is a separate task.

questions.stem: Which is a biosecurity procedure used at Australia's borders?
options: Releasing biological control agents into the gardens around international airports
Vaccinating every incoming traveller against diseases that affect crops and animals
Spraying every imported item with antibiotics to kill any viruses on its surface
Screening bags and mail with detector dogs and X-rays
questions.explanation: Detector dogs, X-ray machines, declarations and inspections intercept risky items such as fruit, seeds, meat and soil. Antibiotics do not kill viruses, and travellers are not vaccinated against plant diseases.

questions.stem: Why are imported animals, such as horses and pet dogs, held in quarantine in Australia before release?
options: To breed them with local animals before they reach their owners
To detect any disease before the animals mix with Australian animals
To let the animals adjust to Australia's climate before release
To give them vaccines against Australian native diseases only
questions.explanation: A period of isolation and testing allows diseases that are incubating to show up or be detected, so infected animals can be treated or refused before they can spread disease.

questions.stem: Foot-and-mouth disease is absent from Australia. Why would an outbreak lead to an immediate national standstill on livestock movements?
options: The disease is spread only by mosquitoes, which travel long distances with livestock
The virus spreads easily on animals and vehicles, so a standstill limits it
Livestock must rest in one place for several days before they can make antibodies
A standstill lets the virus die out in meat that is being transported around the country
questions.explanation: Foot-and-mouth disease is highly contagious and spreads through animal contact and on people, vehicles and equipment, so halting movement contains it while infected properties are identified. It is not mosquito-borne.

questions.stem: Why does Australia carry out surveillance for exotic pests and diseases across northern Australia, including the Torres Strait?
options: Pests and diseases can survive only in the tropical climate of the north
Every one of Australia's imports arrives through ports in the north
It is close to countries where many of these pests occur
Northern Australia has no native species that need to be protected
questions.explanation: Northern Australia is the nearest part of the country to regions where pests such as exotic fruit flies and screw-worm fly occur, so early detection there allows a fast response. Pests can spread far beyond the tropics once established.

questions.stem: Varroa mite was detected near Newcastle in 2022. Movement zones, hive destruction and surveillance were used, but the mite kept spreading, and the national response shifted from eradication to management. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The mite was eradicated, so management of honey bee hives is no longer required
Quarantine slowed the spread, but eradication fails once a pest is widely established
Quarantine measures made no difference at all to how far the mite was able to spread
Destroying hives is always the best way to eradicate a pest that is already established
questions.explanation: Movement controls and hive destruction can limit spread, but once a pest occurs at many sites, including in wild colonies, eradication becomes impractical and the goal becomes managing its impact. The shift to management shows the mite was not eradicated.

questions.stem: Chytrid fungus, which has caused declines in many frog species, spreads in water and on wet equipment. Which procedure should researchers use when moving between field sites?
options: Spray each stream with insecticide before sampling the frogs
Vaccinate frogs at each site before handling them
Disinfect boots and equipment, and use fresh gloves for each frog
Move frogs from one site to another to mix the populations
questions.explanation: Hygiene protocols stop researchers carrying fungal spores between sites and between frogs. Moving frogs between sites would risk spreading the disease, and chytrid is a fungus, not an insect.

questions.stem: Hendra virus spreads from flying foxes to horses, and from infected horses to people. Which measure most directly limits transmission to people?
options: Planting fruit trees close to horse paddocks
Treating flying foxes with an antiviral drug
Vaccinating horses against Hendra virus
Giving antibiotics to people who handle horses
questions.explanation: People have caught Hendra virus only from infected horses, so vaccinating horses breaks the chain to humans. Antibiotics have no action against viruses, and fruit trees attract flying foxes.

questions.stem: Phytophthora dieback is caused by a soil-borne pathogen that kills many native plants. In some national parks, tracks are closed in wet weather and walkers must clean their boots at hygiene stations. How effective is this approach likely to be?
options: It reduces spread on boots, but water and animals still spread it
It removes the pathogen from soil in areas where it is already established
It is pointless, because the pathogen spreads only by spores carried on the wind
It cures plants along the tracks that are already infected by the pathogen
questions.explanation: Phytophthora moves in infested soil and water, so cleaning boots and closing tracks reduces human-assisted spread, but runoff and animals still carry it, and it persists in infested soil. The measures prevent spread rather than cure.

questions.stem: Which is a biological strategy for controlling an invasive species?
options: Building exclusion fences around a nature reserve
Laying poison baits for foxes and wild dogs
Shooting feral goats from helicopters
Releasing myxoma virus to reduce rabbit numbers
questions.explanation: Biological control uses a living natural enemy, such as a pathogen, predator or parasite, to reduce a pest. Fences and shooting are physical methods, and poison baits are chemical.

questions.stem: In the 1920s, the moth Cactoblastis cactorum was introduced to control prickly pear in Queensland and New South Wales. Why is this considered a successful biological control?
options: Its larvae cleared vast areas of prickly pear without harming native plants
Its larvae fed on every invasive weed in Australia as well as on the prickly pear
It removed the need for any other method of weed control anywhere in Australia
It preyed on the cane toads that had been spreading prickly pear seeds through the bush
questions.explanation: The moth's larvae tunnel through prickly pear pads, and within a few years millions of hectares were cleared. A good biological control agent is specific to its target, as this one proved to be in Australia.

questions.stem: After myxoma virus was released in 1950, more than 90% of infected rabbits died at first, but over the following decades death rates fell. Which explains this?
options: Resistant rabbits survived and bred, and milder virus strains spread
The government gradually removed the virus from the environment over time
Rabbits learned to hide from the mosquitoes and fleas that carry the virus
Rabbits made antibodies during their lives and passed them on in their genes
questions.explanation: Natural selection favoured rabbits with genetic resistance, and virus strains that killed hosts less quickly were spread more, because living rabbits are bitten by more vectors. Antibodies made during life are not inherited through genes.

questions.stem: Why is the cane toad considered an example of a failed biological control?
options: It controlled the beetles so well that the sugar cane crops then failed
It died out soon after release because the climate was too cold for it
It was too expensive to breed in the numbers that were needed
It did not control the target beetles and became a serious pest itself
questions.explanation: Cane toads did not reduce cane beetles, partly because the beetles live high on cane stalks and in soil, and the toads spread across northern Australia, harming native predators. A biological control should target only the pest.

questions.stem: Baits containing 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate) are used to control foxes and wild dogs. Why can they be used in parts of Western Australia with less risk to many native animals?
options: Many native animals there are tolerant, because local plants contain the same toxin
Native animals there cannot smell the baits, so they never come close to eating them
1080 affects only introduced mammals and has no effect on any native species
The baits are hung high in trees where only foxes and wild dogs can reach them
questions.explanation: Some Western Australian plants naturally contain fluoroacetate, and native animals that evolved eating them have high tolerance, while introduced foxes are very sensitive. 1080 can still poison some native animals, so it is not specific.

questions.stem: Predator-proof fences protect reserves from which foxes and cats have been removed. What is a limitation of this physical control?
options: It poisons the native animals that live inside the fenced area
Foxes evolve resistance to fences within a few generations
It increases the number of foxes breeding inside the reserve
It protects only the fenced area and needs constant maintenance
questions.explanation: Fences work well for the area inside them, but they are costly to build and maintain, can be breached by floods or fallen trees, and do nothing for land outside. They are a physical barrier, not a poison.

questions.stem: Which approach is most likely to give lasting control of a widely established invasive species?
options: Combining physical, chemical and biological methods with ongoing monitoring
Relying on one chemical applied once at a very high dose over the whole area
Introducing several new predator species to hunt the invasive species
Waiting for native predators to adapt to the invasive species unaided
questions.explanation: Integrated pest management combines methods so that each covers the others' weaknesses, and monitoring shows whether control is working. Introducing new predators risks creating new invasive species, as with the cane toad.

questions.stem: Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus escaped from a quarantine trial on Wardang Island in South Australia in 1995 and spread across the mainland. What does this event show about biological control agents?
options: Viruses cannot spread between rabbits unless they are released deliberately by people
Quarantine on islands always contains a biological agent until it is officially released
Once released, an agent may spread beyond the intended area and cannot be recalled
Biological control agents work only on islands and cannot affect mainland populations
questions.explanation: The virus is thought to have been carried off the island by insects, showing that living agents can spread on their own and that release decisions are hard to reverse. This is why agents are tested thoroughly for host specificity first.

questions.stem: How do national parks help maintain biodiversity?
options: They protect habitat from clearing, so species and ecosystems persist
They remove every predator from the park so that prey species are able to increase
They keep all people out, including scientists, so ecosystems are never disturbed
They replace native vegetation with fast-growing plantations that hold more animals
questions.explanation: Protecting habitat is the most direct way to conserve species, genetic diversity and ecosystem processes. Parks are managed for pests and fire and often allow research and visitors.

questions.stem: In the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, about a third of the area is zoned as no-take 'green zones'. Which effect would researchers expect to find in these zones?
options: Fewer fish, because fishing normally helps fish populations to grow
No coral bleaching, because bleaching is caused mainly by fishing
More invasive species, because no fishing is allowed in these zones
Larger, more numerous fish, with some spilling over into fished areas
questions.explanation: Without fishing, targeted species live longer, grow larger and produce more young, and some adults and larvae move into nearby fished areas. Bleaching is caused mainly by high water temperatures, not fishing.

questions.stem: Why can't marine reserves on their own protect coral reef biodiversity?
options: Corals are unable to grow or reproduce inside protected marine areas
Reserves are always too small to contain a single complete population
Threats such as warming oceans and runoff from land cross reserve boundaries
Fishing is allowed without limit everywhere inside the marine reserves
questions.explanation: Reserves control activities such as fishing within their boundaries, but rising sea temperatures, ocean acidification and sediment and nutrient runoff come from outside. Reserves must be combined with action on these wider threats.

questions.stem: Why do conservation planners try to link national parks with corridors of native vegetation?
options: Corridors increase inbreeding, which strengthens the populations in parks
Corridors reduce the total area of habitat that animals have to defend
Animals can move between parks, keeping gene flow and allowing range shifts
Corridors keep every invasive species out of the parks that they connect
questions.explanation: Corridors let individuals disperse, so isolated populations exchange alleles and can recolonise areas or shift their ranges as the climate changes. Corridors can also be used by pests, so they do not keep them out.

questions.stem: Over 30 years, a small national park surrounded by farmland has lost several species, while a large park connected to other bushland has lost none. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Large parks lose species more slowly only because they receive fewer visitors
Farmland around a park provides better habitat than the park itself does
Species in the small park evolved into new species and were not counted
Small isolated parks hold small populations prone to local extinction
questions.explanation: Small, isolated reserves support small populations with no immigration to replace losses, so chance events, inbreeding and edge effects lead to local extinctions. Size and connectivity are key to a reserve's value.

questions.stem: The eastern quoll is extinct on mainland Australia but survives in Tasmania. Quolls from Tasmania have been released at managed mainland sites. What is a key benefit of this reintroduction?
options: Removing the need to control foxes at the release sites
Creating a new species that is adapted to the mainland
Restoring a lost native predator and its role in the ecosystem
Increasing genetic diversity in the Tasmanian population
questions.explanation: Reintroducing a locally extinct species restores its ecological role, such as eating insects and small animals, and spreads the species' risk across more sites. Fox control is still needed, because foxes prey on quolls.

questions.stem: Reintroduced animals of a locally extinct species often die soon after release in areas where foxes and cats are common. What does this show about reintroduction programs?
options: The threats that caused the extinction must be controlled before release
Animals of reintroduced species are unable to breed in the wild
Animals bred in captivity are always healthier than wild animals
Foxes and cats hunt only animals that have been reintroduced
questions.explanation: If the causes of the original loss remain, released animals face the same fate, so successful programs control predators, restore habitat and monitor survival. Many reintroduced animals do breed once threats are managed.

questions.stem: Scientists propose reviving the thylacine by editing the genome of a living relative, the fat-tailed dunnart. What is a major biological limitation of this plan?
options: The thylacine's DNA sequence is completely unknown to scientists
Dunnarts and thylacines are so alike that no genes would need editing
Edited genes can never be inherited by the offspring of edited animals
Only a few animals with low genetic diversity could be made at first
questions.explanation: Even if successful, a revived population would start from very few animals with limited genetic variation, making it vulnerable to inbreeding and disease. The thylacine genome has been sequenced from preserved specimens, and dunnarts differ from it greatly.

questions.stem: Which is an ethical issue raised by attempts to bring back an extinct species?
options: Extinct species have no DNA left, so the experiments could never begin at all
Revived species would be identical to living species, so they have no value
Bringing back a species is illegal because extinct species have no legal status
Animal welfare, and funds diverted from living threatened species
questions.explanation: De-extinction involves experimental procedures on surrogate animals with uncertain welfare outcomes, and money spent on it might achieve more if used to protect species that still exist. Questions of release, ownership and ecological risk also arise.

questions.stem: The mountain pygmy possum population at Mount Buller had become small and inbred. Males from a genetically different population were introduced, and the population grew. What is this approach called, and why did it work?
options: Cloning; copies of the healthiest males replaced the inbred males in the population
Selective breeding; only the largest possums were allowed to breed with each other
Genetic drift; random changes removed the harmful alleles from the population
Genetic rescue; new alleles reduced inbreeding and improved survival and breeding
questions.explanation: Bringing in unrelated individuals adds new alleles, so offspring are less likely to be homozygous for harmful recessive alleles and are fitter. This deliberate gene flow is called genetic rescue.

questions.stem: Why do captive breeding programs for threatened species keep studbooks recording each animal's ancestry?
options: To track how many offspring are sold to private collectors
To match animals that carry the same alleles so offspring are uniform
To pair unrelated animals, keeping inbreeding low and diversity high
To make sure that only the largest animals in the program are bred
questions.explanation: Knowing pedigrees lets managers pair animals that are least related, so the captive population keeps as much genetic diversity as possible for later release. Pairing animals with the same alleles would increase inbreeding.

questions.stem: Which measurement would best show whether a conservation program has improved the genetic diversity of a threatened population?
options: Comparing heterozygosity in DNA samples taken before and after the program
Counting the number of animals seen during one survey at the end of the program
Measuring the average body mass of the animals before and after the program
Recording how many visitors saw the animals while the program was running
questions.explanation: Genetic diversity is measured directly from DNA, for example as the proportion of loci at which individuals are heterozygous. Population size and body condition can change without any change in genetic diversity.

questions.stem: How do seed banks support the conservation of threatened plant species?
options: They remove the need to protect the natural habitats of the plants
They store seed from many plants, keeping genetic diversity
They store one seed of each species so that the species can be cloned later
They plant every stored seed each year so that the seeds stay alive
questions.explanation: Collecting seed from many plants across a species' range preserves a wide sample of its alleles, which can be used to restore populations if wild ones are lost. Habitat protection is still needed for plants to survive in the wild.

questions.stem: Which is a human-induced selection pressure on biodiversity?
options: A drought caused by a natural El Nino cycle
A meteorite impact that starts a large fire
Climate change driven by greenhouse gas emissions
A volcanic eruption that buries a forest in ash
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gas emissions from human activity are warming the climate, which shifts the conditions species must cope with. Eruptions, natural climate cycles and meteorites are natural pressures.

questions.stem: Ocean temperatures on a reef are projected to keep rising, causing more frequent coral bleaching. What is the most likely long-term effect on reef biodiversity?
options: An increase in all coral species, because warm water speeds up the growth of corals
Full recovery after every event, because corals always regrow quickly between events
Replacement of the existing corals by entirely new coral species within one year
Loss of heat-sensitive corals and their dependants, favouring tolerant species
questions.explanation: Frequent heat stress acts as a selection pressure: sensitive species die and do not have time to recover between events, while heat-tolerant species are favoured, reducing diversity and changing the reef. New species do not evolve within a year.

questions.stem: Rising temperatures are allowing an invasive weed to spread further south each decade. What is the most likely effect on native plant communities in newly invaded areas?
options: Native plants grow faster because the weed adds nutrients
The weed evolves into a native species within a decade
Native plants become resistant to the weed straight away
Native plants are outcompeted, so species diversity falls
questions.explanation: Invasive weeds often grow and spread faster than native plants, taking light, water and space, so native species decline. Native plants cannot evolve resistance immediately, and an introduced species does not become native.
